4033-who-spoke-next:
A story told by objects in an old garret turns to a musket with an old republican pride, a weapon that speaks in one short, decided word. Boys Frank and Harry call on their mother for its history, and she reports the musket's scorn for palaver.

The musket recalls service beside the Boston Cadets, the governor's body guard, when crowds of women and children pressed so close that the governor could hardly move. Flourished round bravely by its master, it did bloody work yet felt defiled as never before. The tale charms young readers with a talking relic of American history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sext:
Sext, the sixth hour of the Roman day, matches our noon closely. Among Jews it already ranked with Terce and None as an hour most favorable to prayer, and Acts tells how Peter went up to pray at that hour. It was midday, the usual hour of rest, and so a natural pause for prayer. This entry gathers the Fathers' symbolism of the hour, summarized from Cardinal Bona's work on psalmody.

Noon is the hour of the sun at its full, an image of divine splendor and grace. At the sixth hour Abraham received the three angels, image of the Trinity, and Adam and Eve ate the fatal apple. Ambrose urged prayer at noon because divine light then stands at its fullest. Above all, it was the hour Christ was nailed to the cross, a memory that left a visible mark on most of the liturgy for this hour.

papyrus-of-ani-1913-text:
The Papyrus of Ani, in its 1913 text edition, presents Egypt's most famous Book of the Dead. Ani was a royal scribe in ancient Thebes. His painted scroll guided his soul through the afterlife.

Translator Wallis Budge renders the spells, hymns, and judgment scenes. The dead man's heart is weighed against a feather of truth. Gods, demons, and gates crowd the path to paradise. Budge's versions shaped how the West first read these texts. The scroll remains a funerary treasure, and this edition keeps a classic translation in reach. Its painted scenes remain icons of Egyptian faith.
what-katy-did-next: Here the reader finds a frontispiece note, a dedication, and a contents list, but no chapter text. Susan Coolidge wrote What Katy Did Next for the many girls who begged for more of Katy Carr. Twelve years of pleas, her dedication says, brought the book about. The contents start with a surprise guest and an invitation. Katy then sails on a ship called the Spartacus. Later chapters tour England, cross the Channel, and reach Rome for a holiday.
who-spoke-next:
Mrs. Follen wrote Who Spoke Next, a set of tales in which household things tell their own stories. Frank and Harry call on their mother for the tale of the old musket, as promised. The musket, she says, was proud and slow to speak. It had made itself heard in the world by one short, sharp word.

Deeds, not words, the musket declares, is the motto for all. It recalls no clear sense of life before human craft shaped its parts. Each part, it insists, was perfect of its kind. Follen lets an old gun tell of war and years in a garret. Young readers learn matter and memory from a talking thing.
